paper_title: Nested Sparsity for Scalable Pretraining and Continual Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) transformers, the standard backbone for modern large-scale deep learning, employ conditional computation: only a sparse subset of model weights is used in each forward pass. In MoE transformers, this sparsity arises in the MoE operator, which generalizes the multi-layer perceptron in the classical transformer. In this work, we explore an alternative mechanism for conditional computation that analogously generalizes the attention operator. The sparsity induced by this mechanism naturally nests (i.e., hierarchically composes) with the sparsity induced by the MoE operator. We show that a transformer employing this nested sparsity mechanism, which we call Nestor, performs better than a conventional MoE transformer at equal compute and equal sparsity in language model pretraining. We also show that Nestor is well-suited for continual pretraining: it can be adapted to longer contexts more effectively than conventional MoEs, as well as adapt more efficiently to new domains while forgetting less on old domains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these benefits persist as model size, dataset size, and context length grow. Our results demonstrate the potential of alternative conditional computation mechanisms for deep neural network architectures. Code and checkpoints are available on GitHub at https://github.com/Ma-Lab-Berkeley/Nestor .

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Conditional computation in LLMs. Large language models (LLMs) based on variants of the transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) improve predictably as their parameters, training data, and training compute grow (Kaplan et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). central goal of architecture design is to reach lower loss with the same training compute. particularly successful approach is conditional computation (Bengio et al., 2013; Shazeer et al., 2017), in which each input uses only small (input-dependent) active subset of the model weights and correspondingly less compute for training or inference. In this setting, the number of total parameters grows much faster than the active parameters and compute used on each token. Mixtures of experts (MoEs). In modern LLMs, this form of conditional computation is implemented almost exclusively via the MoE operator (Jacobs et al., 1991; Shazeer et al., 2017; Lepikhin et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2022), which replaces the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) in each transformer layer by many expert MLPs and routes each token to few of them. As result, many modern LLMs are MoE transformers (Jiang et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Kimi Team, 2025a; OpenAI, 2025). In all of these models, however, this conditional computation is confined to the MLP weights: every token is processed by the same attention parameters in every layer. The attention operator accounts for considerable fraction of the (active) parameters used by each token, and at long context lengths it accounts for most of the computation. One may then ask whether conditional computation can be applied to the attention operator as well, and how it should interact with the MoE. Sparsity in the attention operator. Attention operators traditionally implement two forms of conditional computation. The more popular by far is the so-called sparse attention methods, which reduce the cost of attention by restricting the set of tokens to which each token attends, via fixed local patterns (Child et al., 2019; Beltagy et al., 2020), hashing or clustering (Kitaev et al., 2020; Roy et al., 2021), or top-K selection for each query (Yuan et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; DeepSeek-AI, 2025). Relatedly, many LLMs interleave few global attention layers with cheaper local or linear attention layers (Brown et al., 2020; Gemma Team, 2025; Kimi Team, 2025b). These methods sparsify the attention map, with the purpose of approximating full attention at lower cost, while all tokens still share the same attention parameters. Other methods restrict the set of parameters used by each token, such as mixtures of attention heads (Zhang et al., 2022; Csordas et al., 2024), which route each token to subset of the attention parameters, while every token still attends to the whole context. Other methods make both the map and the parameters sparse (Piekos et al., 2025), or pair mixtures of attention heads with an MoE (Shen et al., 2023; Csordas et al., 2024). In each of them, the attention is routed separately from the MLP and anew in every layer. Continual pretraining. One of the circumstances in which such attention sparsity is most effective at reducing both training and inference costs is with long context documents. Pretrained models are routinely continually (pre-)trained in long-context extension stage (Xiong et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Grattafiori et al., 2024), and simultaneously further on new domains, such as code and mathematics (Gururangan et al., 2020; Rozi`ere et al., 2023; Azerbayev et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024). Since neural networks trained on new distribution tend to perform worse on the old one (McCloskey et al., 1989; French, 1999; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017), and LLMs are no exception (Luo et al., 2025), central challenge is to maintain the performance on old data while capably handling the new data. 2 Our contributions. We propose NESTOR (Figure 1), transformer architecture with nested sparsity: we generalize the attention operator in the same way that the MoE operator generalizes the MLP, and hierarchically composes the two resultant operators sparsity. This yields natural architecture that generalizes MoE transformers and has three coupled but distinct forms of sparsity: attention weight sparsity, attention map sparsity, and expert sparsity. We study it empirically and theoretically in language model pretraining and continual pretraining, showing that NESTOR architectures utilizing all sparsity axes in tandem outperform strong MoE and dense Transformer baselines at scales from 100M to 1B active parameters, at the limit of our compute resources. Namely, our contributions are: Compute-efficient pretraining (Section 3). We perform scaling law study, finding that NESTOR is 1.131.29 as compute-efficient as the MoE transformer, and 3.14.1 as compute-efficient as dense transformer; neither factor shrinks as the scale grows. Effective continual pretraining (Section 4). When adapted to various specialized domains, we show that NESTOR gains about as much as the MoE transformer on every new domain while forgetting less of the pretraining distribution, with fewer training FLOPs per token in the continual pretraining data. When extended from context length of 4k to lengths up to 64k, NESTOR preserves its advantage over the MoE transformer when each model receives an equal number of continual pretraining tokens, and its advantage over the MoE transformer grows at longer context lengths when each model uses equal continual pretraining FLOPs. Theoretical analysis (Section 5). We give theoretical account of these observations. Namely, we give statistical model of data with hierarchical latent structure, in which stylized version of NESTOR outperforms stylized version of an MoE transformer. We show that this analytically tractable model reproduces the pretraining compute efficiency, its growth with the context length, and the reduced forgetting that we observe empirically. Overall, our results suggest that conditional computation need not be confined to the MLP, and that adding and composing new sparsity mechanisms is promising direction for architecture design. We postpone detailed discussion of related work to Appendix A.

Conditional computation in MoE transformers. Each layer of transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) updates the token features x1, . . . , xS RD using an attention operator, which mixes information across tokens, followed by an MLP, which acts on each token separately. One layer stores attention operators and CE experts, while token uses Kc and KcKe of them respectively. Each layer also has small number CEs of experts whose weights are tied across columns (cf. the shared experts of Dai et al. (2024)). NESTOR as meta-architecture. We group the layers of the network into blocks of layers each, and compute the column routing once per block, from the input of the block, so that token stays in the same columns for all layers within the block (see Figure 1a left). Within block, each column is small MoE transformer of depth whose attention operates on its own subsequence; the columns of token share the input to each layer (Appendix B). Apart from the shared experts, the routers, and the residual connections, token uses only the parameters of its Kc columns. Setting = 1 in (2) and (3) recovers the regular MoE transformer exactly, and further setting = 1 recovers the dense transformer, so conventional transformers are special cases of NESTOR. Actually, at the expense of slightly more inefficient implementation, we can use any sequence-to-sequence deep architecture for each column. Thus, one can view NESTOR as metaarchitecture for sparsely and hierarchically composing parallel deep networks, such that the presented version is special case. Relation to sparse attention. Sparse attention methods restrict the set of tokens to which each token attends (the attention pattern) to reduce the cost of long contexts. The pattern may be fixed in advance, as in sliding window attention and its variants (Child et al., 2019; Beltagy et al., 2020); computed by clustering the tokens (Roy et al., 2021); or selected for each query by top-K rule over blocks or tokens (Yuan et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; DeepSeek-AI, 2025). In all of these methods every token is processed by the same attention parameters, so only the pattern is conditional, and the purpose is to approximate full attention at lower cost. Mixtures of attention heads (Zhang et al., 2022; Csordas et al., 2024) route each token to subset of the attention parameters, and each token still attends to the full context. Column-routed attention (2) is sparse in both senses: one routing decision determines both the parameters that the token uses and the tokens to which it attends. The closest mechanism is that of Piekos et al. (2025), in which each attention head selects fixed number of tokens and attends only among them. There, the selection is made by the heads, separately in every layer, and is independent of the MLP; in NESTOR, the selection is made by the tokens, once per block, and the selected module contains the attention operators and the experts of all layers. This makes the sparsity nested. The two approaches can be combined, because any sparse attention pattern (or, again, any backbone network) can be applied within column. In this work each column uses full causal attention over its tokens; the baselines in Sections 3 and 4 also use full causal attention. We discuss the relation of NESTOR to such related work further and in detail in Appendix A. 4 Further design choices. We summarize the remaining empirical design choices here, with more details in Appendix C. Sparsity schedule. The number of active columns Kc can differ between blocks. In all experiments we use = 8 and increase Kc with depth, from Kc = 3 in the first block to Kc = in the last block, which computes full attention over the whole sequence. Hence, this architecture relates to the interleaved globalized and local (or linear) attention layers popular in modern LLMs (Brown et al., 2020; Gemma Team, 2025; Kimi Team, 2025b); here, one can interpret NESTOR as using progressively more globalized attention layers. Our experimental baselines use global attention at each layer, therefore using more attention compute than NESTOR. Residual connections. Equations (2) and (3) show plain residual connections. In NESTOR, each active column accumulates its outputs in its own residual stream. The streams are combined, within and across blocks, by an attention residual (Kimi Team, 2026): the input of each layer is learned softmaxweighted mixture of the token embedding, the outputs of the earlier blocks, and the mean of the streams of the current block. The input of the output head also includes the deviation of each stream from the mean. We ablate this choice in Appendix C.3; note that our baselines also use and benefit from attention residuals. Routing. Both routers use top-K selection by each token, and are balanced without an auxiliary loss by bias that is updated in backpropagation-free manner (Wang et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024). We ablate our routing and sparsity setup in Appendix C.3. We fully describe the final architecture in Appendix B. Aspirational connection to the cerebral cortex. To some extent, one may view NESTOR as an architecture that tries to emulate the neural architecture of the cerebral cortex of brain (Hawkins, 2021): the blocks correspond to different lobes or functional regions in the cortex, from low-level to high-level, and the many columns in each block emulate the cortical columns within each region.

sections.title: 3 Compute-Efficient Pretraining with NESTOR
sections.content: In this section we show that NESTOR is more compute-efficient than strong iso-sparsity MoE transformer and dense transformer baselines in language model pretraining, and that the advantage does not shrink as the scale grows to the limits of our compute. Following prior scaling law studies of MoE transformers (see Appendix A), we compare architectures at the same sparsity, fit scaling law to each, and report the projected compute that each baseline needs to reach the held-out loss of NESTOR. Setup. We compare three architectures at four scales, which we call 100M, 200M, 500M, and 1B after the active parameter count. The dense transformer has width {480, 640, 960, 1280}, depth {12, 16, 24, 32}, 16 heads, and MLP width 4D. The MoE transformer has the same shape, with each MLP replaced by = 24 experts of which Ke = 3 are active, so that its active MLP width is also 4D. NESTOR uses = 8 columns, increasing with depth from Kc = 3 in the first block to Kc = 8 (all columns active) in the final block. Both baselines use full causal attention with the attention residual (Kimi Team, 2026). At each scale, NESTOR uses no more training FLOPs than either baseline,1 and stores approximately the same number of parameters as the MoE transformer. We consider further baselines in Appendix C.3. All models are trained on DCLM-baseline (Li et al., 2024) at context length = 4096 for 50 tokens per active parameter (beyond the roughly 20 that are compute optimal for dense transformers; Hoffmann et al., 2022).The parameterization and optimizer settings used in these experiments are specified in Appendix D. sections.title: 4 NESTOR Enables Efficient Continual Learning
sections.content: A pretrained model is often customized via continual training to learn new capabilities while retaining old ones. Concretely, pretrained models are often continually pre-trained on new domains (Gururangan et al., 2020; Rozi`ere et al., 2023; Azerbayev et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024) and longer contexts (Xiong et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Grattafiori et al., 2024); in this setting, it is important to retain its original capabilities on old domains and shorter contexts, which continual training tends to erode (French, 1999; Luo et al., 2025). In this section we show that NESTOR is well suited to both settings: it adapts to new domains as well as the MoE transformer while forgetting less (Section 4.1), and it extends to long contexts more efficiently and effectively (Section 4.2).

sections.title: 4.1 Domain Adaptation
sections.content: Setup. We compare the 500M NESTOR, 500M MoE transformer, and 1B dense transformer, selected for their similar pretraining losses. All models first undergo context extension to 32k using equal token budgets on DCLM. Details of the starting checkpoints and their initial performance are in Appendix C.4. Each model is then trained separately on 0.5B tokens from each of four target domains, without replay of pretraining data (a common way to reduce forgetting; Ibrahim et al., 2024): books (PG-19; Rae et al., 2020), mathematics (OpenWebMath; Paster et al., 2024), code (AlgebraicStack; Azerbayev et al., 2024), and German (FineWeb2; Penedo et al., 2025). We freeze the router parameters of both sparse models (cf. Li et al., 2025) and update all remaining trainable parameters; the dense model is fully fine-tuned. We measure adaptation by the reduction in held-out loss on the target corpus and forgetting by the increase in held-out loss on the pretraining corpus, both relative to the model before adaptation. We also repeat the experiment with 25% of the training tokens drawn from the pretraining corpus, keeping the total budget fixed at 0.5B tokens; details and results are in Appendix C.4. Table 6 reports the held-out losses before and after adaptation. NESTOR adapts as well as the baselines with less forgetting. All three models achieve similar adaptation gains: averaged across the four target domains, the gains of NESTOR and the 1B dense transformer are both within 1% of the 500M MoE transformers (Figure 3). The models differ more in how much they forget. NESTOR forgets 3% less than the MoE on average, whereas the dense model forgets 21%. sections.title: 4.2 Long Context Extension
sections.content: Setup. Starting from the pretrained models of Section 3, which have context length 4k, we extend each model to target context length {8k, 16k, 32k, 64k} by continued pretraining on long documents (Xiong et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025) of at least tokens from DCLM-baseline. Each target length is separate run from the 4k checkpoint. The baselines are trained on 0.5B tokens. Since the FLOPs per token of NESTOR decrease relative to the baselines as grows (Figure 10), we train NESTOR in two settings: at equal tokens (0.5B), and at equal FLOPs, where the saved compute is spent on more tokens of either repeated or new documents. We report the held-out loss at length S, relative to the MoE transformer of the same scale. Details of the data, the schedules, and the losses behind Figure 4 are provided in Appendix C.5. The advantage of NESTOR grows with context length at equal compute. At equal tokens, NESTOR achieves gains from context extension comparable to those of the MoE transformer, broadly preserving its advantage before extension (Figure 4). As the context length increases, its lower FLOPs per token allow more training within the same compute budget (Figure 10). Spending these savings on repeated data produces downward trend in held-out loss relative to MoE, even without additional training data. Spending them on fresh data, as one might expect, yields the largest improvements. In Appendix we quantify the saving: for equal shapes and balanced routing, at equal FLOPs NESTOR trains on R(S) = (S0 + S)/(S0 + ρS) times as many tokens as the MoE, where ρ is the mean fraction Kc/C of active columns and S0 the context length at which the MoE transformers attention FLOPs equal its other FLOPs, and R(S) increases with towards 1/ρ.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we introduced nested sparsity, conditional computation mechanism in which router sends each token to several columns, and each column contains its own attention operators and its own experts. The resulting architecture, NESTOR, generalizes both the MoE transformer and the dense transformer. In language model pretraining at scales from 100M to 1B active parameters, the MoE transformer needs 1.13 1.29 the compute of NESTOR to reach the same loss at an equal number of stored parameters, and this factor shows no downward trend as the scale grows (Section 3). In continual pretraining, NESTOR adapts to new domains as well as the MoE transformer while forgetting less (Section 4.1), and its advantage in long context extension grows with the context length at equal FLOPs (Section 4.2). Our theoretical analysis (Section 5) provides conceptual reasoning for why NESTOR can obtain such empirical results in the context of highly structured data. Our study has several limitations, which suggest directions for future work. First, our largest model has 1B active parameters, and we evaluate models by their held-out loss; an important next step is to test whether the compute multiplier persists at larger scales and carries over to downstream tasks, such as standard benchmarks after post-training. Second, NESTOR is in some sense meta-architecture, and we studied only the case in which each column uses full causal attention. Columns with sparse or linear attention would compound the savings at long contexts. More broadly, columns comprised of subnetworks with interesting properties could preserve them through the meta-architecture. 2Here, the map is in some sense redundant: freezing it would remove this forgetting without changing the function class. Proposition 2 compares the predictors with attention and expert weights trained, as in Section 4.1.

sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: Scaling laws and sparsity. The loss of language model is well described by power law in the number of parameters, the number of training tokens, and the training compute (Kaplan et al., 2020), which determines the compute-optimal allocation between model size and data (Hoffmann et al., 2022). Several works extend these laws to MoE transformers. Clark et al. (2022) fit law that is jointly function of the model size and the number of experts. Ludziejewski et al. (2024) add the granularity of the experts as variable, and find that MoE transformers with appropriately sized experts outperform dense transformers at every compute budget. Abnar et al. (2025) study the sparsity level, i.e., the fraction of inactive parameters, and find that the optimal sparsity increases with the model size, and Ludziejewski et al. (2025) fit joint law for dense and MoE models under memory constraints. In all of these works only the MLP is sparse. Since our architectures are sparse in more than one component, we compare them at the same sparsity to avoid ambiguity in the scaling laws: we fit scaling law for each architecture and report the projected compute efficiency compared to strong MoE transformer baseline to reach the same held-out loss. Conditional computation and mixtures of experts. Mixtures of experts were introduced by Jacobs et al. (1991), and Jordan et al. (1994) extended them to tree of gating networks. Shazeer et al. (2017) used them as sparsely gated layer in deep networks, following the proposal of conditional computation (Bengio et al., 2013), and later work used them in the transformer and changed the routing (Lepikhin et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022). Recent MoE transformers use many small experts, some of which are shared by all tokens (Dai et al., 2024), and balance the load of the experts with bias in the router (Wang et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024); we do the same. Nested sparsity is closest to the hierarchical mixture of experts, since in NESTOR the experts of token are selected from the experts of its columns, which are in turn selected by the column router. The difference is that in hierarchical mixture of experts both levels of routing select MLPs, whereas in NESTOR the first level selects an attention operator together with its context, and this selection is held fixed over several layers. Other works route tokens around whole layers: in Raposo et al. (2024) only the top-K tokens of each layer go through its attention operator and MLP, and Ainslie et al. (2023) apply heavy attention operator and MLP only to the routed tokens and light one to all tokens. In these methods there is single routed module per layer, and token that is not selected does not go through it; in NESTOR, every layer applies to every token, with modules that depend on the token. Sparse attention and mixtures of attention heads. large body of work reduces the quadratic cost of attention by making the attention map sparse. The pattern can be fixed in advance, such as local or strided windows (Child et al., 2019; Beltagy et al., 2020); it can depend on the content through hashing or clustering of the queries and keys (Kitaev et al., 2020; Roy et al., 2021); or it can be selected for each query by top-K rule over blocks or tokens (Yuan et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; DeepSeek-AI, 2025). complementary line of work makes the attention parameters sparse, by routing each token to subset of the attention heads or of their projections (Zhang et al., 2022; Csordas et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025), possibly together with an MoE operator for the MLP (Shen et al., 2023). The method of Piekos et al. (2025), in which fixed number of tokens is selected for each head and attention is computed only among them, is the closest to column-routed attention. We compare NESTOR with these methods in detail in Section 2. In column-routed attention, both the pattern and the parameters are sparse, and both are given by one routing decision, which is computed for each token, held fixed over block of layers, and shared with the experts. Also, in our experiments NESTOR has lower loss than baselines with full attention, which sparse attention methods approximate. Interleaved attention. In many LLMs, the cost of attention is reduced by using full attention in only some of the layers. GPT-3 has dense and locally banded sparse attention layers in alternation (Brown et al., 2020), 15 and more recent models interleave sliding window and global attention layers at ratios from one to one up to five to one (Gemma Team, 2024; Gemma Team, 2025; Cohere, 2025; OpenAI, 2025). In hybrid models, the local layers are state space or linear attention layers (Lieber et al., 2024; MiniMax, 2025; Kimi Team, 2025b). NESTOR uses the same principle with different local operator: the number of active columns increases with depth, so attention in the early blocks is computed within routed subsequences, and attention in the last block is full attention over the whole sequence (Section 2). Unlike sliding window, the context of column depends on the input and can contain tokens from anywhere in the sequence. Continual pretraining and forgetting. Continued pretraining on text from target domain improves performance in that domain (Gururangan et al., 2020), and it is the standard way to obtain specialized models for code and mathematics (Rozi`ere et al., 2023; Azerbayev et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024). Its main difficulty is catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey et al., 1989; French, 1999; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2025), which is usually reduced by replaying pretraining data (Ibrahim et al., 2024). French (1991) observed that forgetting comes from the overlap of distributed representations, and that sparser representations reduce it. For this reason, many continual learning methods use separate parameters for each task, obtained by adding, freezing, or masking parts of the network (Rusu et al., 2016; Fernando et al., 2017; Aljundi et al., 2017; Mallya et al., 2018; Wortsman et al., 2020). For language models, modularity is typically obtained with experts: Gururangan et al. (2022) condition the experts on the domain and adapt to new domain by training new expert with the rest of the model frozen, Chen et al. (2023) add and freeze experts as the distribution changes, Sukhbaatar et al. (2024) train domain models separately and merge their MLPs into the experts of an MoE transformer, and Lin et al. (2025) update sparse set of memory slots. Shen et al. (2023) route tokens among both attention and MLP modules, and find that their model has less forgetting than dense model and that new modules can be added to it. Therien et al. (2025) find that the routing of standard MoE transformers changes little under the distribution shifts of continual pretraining, and Li et al. (2025) analyze MoE models in continual learning theoretically. When an MoE transformer is continually pretrained with trainable attention parameters, these parameters are shared by all tokens, so the gradient of every new token changes them. In NESTOR, each layer applies to token only the attention operators and experts of its columns, in addition to the shared experts, with no task labels and no changes to training. In the one-layer model of Section 5, where each token uses one column, there is then no forgetting on the other coarse labels. Our analysis of forgetting in Section 5 uses the overlap between the row spaces of the value maps of the old and the new data, as in Doan et al. (2021).

Each baseline is the MoE transformer with sliding window attention in place of the column attention of NESTOR, pretrained from scratch at every scale with the same recipe, token budget, and attention residuals as the other models, with single seed. The three baselines differ in how the attention FLOPs are distributed over depth. The first has the depth and the blocks of NESTOR. Third, each token uses more experts of smaller width: at the 200M active parameter scale, token uses 7 to 10 experts per layer in NESTOR, and 3 in the baseline. We test whether these differences, or column-routed attention alone, explain the improvement in Figure 2. The held-out losses of eight models at the 200M active parameter scale and of three models at the 500M scale are in Table 4. sections.title: D Optimization and Initialization
sections.content: Optimization. The matrices of the attention operators and of the experts are trained by Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) with the base learning rate ηM = 0.01. The update of matrix in RDoutDin is multiplied by Dout/Din, so that its spectral norm scales as in the spectral condition of Yang et al. (2023). All other parameters are trained by AdamW (Loshchilov et al., 2019) with the base learning rate ηA = 3 104. These are the token embeddings, the output head, the expert routers of the MoE baseline and of NESTOR (including the routers of the shared experts and of the experts of each column, and the gate (22)), the queries and gains of the attention residual, and the normalization gains. The only exception is the last layer of the column router, which has the learning rate ηA/(Din M), where Din = 128 is the hidden width of the router and is the number of layers in its block: this router is evaluated once and used by all layers, so its gradient is sum of terms. The Muon base learning rate was selected at 200M and reused at the other scales. The AdamW base learning rate was fixed, without separate sweep. Initialization. The three architectures have the same initialization. The query, key, and value projections, the input and gate matrices of the experts, the expert routers, and the gate (22) are initialized with standard 8. The output projections of the attention operators and the output matrices of the experts deviation 0.1/ 2L, where is the number of layers of the model. are initialized with this standard deviation divided by The token embeddings and the output head have standard deviation 0.1; the output of the embedding is multiplied by 12, and the output logits are divided by 8. The last layer of the column router is initialized with standard deviation 1/Din, so that the column routing is close to uniform at initialization, and the queries of the attention residual are initialized at zero. sections.title: E Compute Multipliers under Scaling Laws
sections.content: In addition to Sections 3 and 4.2, this section gives compute accounting for the full architectures, analogous to the one in Theorem 4(c) for Model 1 at fixed model size. We take as hypothesis that the losses of the full architectures follow scaling law with common exponents and coefficients that depend on the architecture.
